entry.title: P2share: how to turn any network (or testnet!) into a bitcoin miner
entry.summary:
The discussion revolves around the security and integrity of blockchain algorithms, particularly in the context of Ethereum's RANDAO block-proposer-choosing mechanism. Ethereum employs a deterministic signature system (BLS) that generates outcomes which are both pseudorandom and unpredictable for those without the key, effectively preventing the possibility of grinding. This system operates by having each validator contribute their signature, which is then incrementally XORed until the epoch concludes after 32 blocks. The final output can only be predicted at the very last step, safeguarding against grinding attacks. However, vulnerabilities such as block withholding and forking still exist. The latter, detailed in [Forking the RANDAO](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/037), presents a fundamental challenge to the proof of stake (PoS) models, traditionally susceptible to what's known as "history grinding" threats or the "nothing at stake" problem.
Deep forking indicates a significant flaw in PoS systems, as they rely on slashing mechanisms to maintain a single canonical chain, which might not be effective in all cases. This has led to reliance on "weak subjectivity" as a defense rather than slashing. The practicality of these attacks remains uncertain, suggesting that real-world applications might still be secure from such exploits. Moreover, the potential for data malleation within blocks exists due to the flexibility in handling external data sources and Turing-complete scripts. This flexibility allows for the reinterpretation of oracle outputs, thus enabling further manipulation of the blockchain's historical and future states. This highlights a broader security concern where control over the narrative, or "history being written by the victors," can lead to alterations in the blockchain's perceived truth, affecting both past and anticipated future transactions.
